analysis.one_liner: Directs the Consumer Product Safety Commission to set a fire-safety standard for lithium-ion batteries in e-bikes and scooters.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared the Senate Commerce Committee in December 2024 but never received a Senate vote before Congress ended, so no federal fire-safety standard for e-bike and scooter batteries was mandated.
analysis.plain_summary: Fires from the rechargeable lithium-ion batteries that power electric bikes and scooters have caused injuries and deaths, and this bill would require the Consumer Product Safety Commission to write a national safety standard for those batteries within 180 days, covering devices like e-bikes and e-scooters. It passed out of the Senate Commerce Committee but never got a vote by the full Senate before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If enacted, the main beneficiaries would be anyone who rides, stores, or lives near e-bikes and e-scooters—especially apartment dwellers and delivery workers, since charging these devices in homes has been a source of deadly fires. Fire departments and insurers would also see fewer battery-fire emergencies.
analysis.who_benefits_short: E-bike riders, apartment dwellers, delivery workers

how_it_helps.text: The bill orders the CPSC to write a consumer product safety standard for the rechargeable lithium-ion batteries used in micromobility devices, aimed at protecting against fires caused by those batteries.

It sets a deadline of 180 days after enactment for the CPSC to finish the standard, and covers electric bicycles and electric scooters, devices whose battery fires have caused deaths and injuries in densely populated cities.

analysis.who_pays: Battery and micromobility device makers would bear the cost of meeting the new federal standard, and some of that cost could be passed to consumers through higher prices for e-bikes and scooters.
analysis.who_pays_short: Battery and e-bike makers, and some device buyers

drawbacks.text: A mandatory safety standard would impose compliance costs on battery makers, importers, and sellers of e-bikes and scooters, which could raise prices for consumers in a market many low- and moderate-income workers rely on for commuting and delivery work.

The bill sets a hard 180-day deadline for the CPSC to issue a final standard, an unusually short window that could force a rushed rule or limit the agency's ability to test different technical approaches before finalizing it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit—fewer deadly battery fires in e-bikes and scooters—is concrete and the cost to manufacturers is a compliance burden common to product safety rules. The main drawbacks are compliance costs that may fall on small importers and sellers, and the possibility that a rigid 180-day deadline produces a rushed standard. On balance the costs are modest against a life-safety gain, and the bill died without those costs ever being tested.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Commerce Committee reported the bill to the Senate floor in December 2024, but the full Senate never voted on it before the Congress ended, so it died on the calendar.

narrative.text: Introduced March 28, 2023 and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee.
On July 31, 2024, the Committee ordered the bill reported favorably without amendment.
On December 17, 2024, the Committee formally reported the bill and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders, meaning it was waiting for floor time.
The 118th Congress ended January 3, 2025 without the Senate taking up the bill; bills left on the calendar when a Congress ends die and must be reintroduced.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Battery and micromobility makers are better off, since they avoid a federal fire-safety mandate; the public never got the promised standard.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Battery and e-bike makers avoid a safety mandate

for.name: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it through the Senate Commerce Committee.

for.name: Sen. Maria Cantwell
for.role: Chair, Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill out of committee without amendment in December 2024, placing it on the Senate calendar.

for.name: Sens. Schumer, Blackburn, Braun, and Tester
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors, giving the bill bipartisan backing.

against.name: Senate Republican and Democratic leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote after it was placed on the legislative calendar in December 2024, allowing it to die when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan from the start—two Democratic and two Republican original cosponsors—and cleared committee without opposition, so its death was not a party-line fight.

industries.industry: E-bike and e-scooter manufacturers and importers
industries.note: They would have to design batteries to meet a mandatory federal fire-safety standard, a compliance cost that could raise prices. The gain for ordinary people is a lower risk of the battery fires that have destroyed homes and killed riders.
Suppliers of compliant lithium-ion cells could gain a market advantage as products must meet the federal standard, while non-compliant suppliers lose access.
